source_title: Eastman Kodak files for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection
publisher_issuer: CNN Money; corroborated by DPReview and Financier Worldwide
company_context: Eastman Kodak invented the first digital camera in 1975 and held over 1,000 digital-imaging patents, yet protected its highly profitable film business and failed to act decisively on the digital transition it had pioneered. As film demand collapsed, revenue fell from ~$13.3 billion (2003) to ~$6 billion (2011), culminating in a Chapter 11 filing on January 19, 2012.
business_type: Imaging and photographic film / digital imaging manufacturer
macro_context: Rapid shift from film to digital photography and then smartphone cameras; 2008 recession; legacy high pension and cost structure.
evidence_summary: Kodak invented digital photography but chose to defend its dominant film franchise rather than cannibalize it with digital, treating digital as a threat to protect against rather than a business to lead. As film demand evaporated, revenue collapsed from ~$13.3 billion (2003, ~64,000 employees) to ~$6 billion (2011, ~17,000 employees). On January 19, 2012 it filed Chapter 11 with assets of $5.1 billion and liabilities of $6.75 billion, citing failure to keep pace with digital, the 2008 recession, and high pension costs.
owner_decision_context: Kodak leadership repeatedly chose to protect the lucrative film business and delay aggressive commitment to digital, despite owning the founding technology and patents, fearing cannibalization of film margins.
action_taken: Defended the legacy film franchise and underinvested in/delayed the digital pivot it had invented (the wrong strategic action), allowing competitors to capture digital while film demand collapsed; the decision deepened distress until Chapter 11.
outcome_evidence: Revenue collapse from ~$13.3B (2003) to ~$6B (2011), workforce shrinking from ~64,000 to ~17,000, and a January 2012 Chapter 11 filing ($5.1B assets vs $6.75B liabilities) confirm the protect-film strategy worsened the company's position.
source_limitations: WebFetch unavailable (403 pattern); figures confirmed across CNN Money, DPReview, and Financier Worldwide via WebSearch snippets. Revenue and headcount figures are reported approximations; the strategic-intent framing (defending film) is drawn from contemporaneous reporting and case analyses, not a single audited disclosure.

inferred: Defending film over leading digital was the strategic decision that deepened the decline (wrong action worsened)

Tests whether the engine identifies a strategic-commitment decision (not lack of capability) as the root cause and routes to strategic-capex/re-evaluation.
